summary: Round 2: the round-1 blocking item is fixed and I found no blocking issues. F9 is now decided only by a real headless Chromium context. checkLogoutInBrowser (scripts/migration/functional/run.mjs:1120) sends login, session, logout and session through in-page fetch with credentials:'include' and redirect:'manual', then judges the jar by what each cookie puts on the wire. The new f9LeftoverReason/f9WirePair (run.mjs:1057-1084) handle the empty name, the key trimmed of SP/HTAB, and raw plus percent-decoded forms. This covers everything Next's parseCookie can read: the key is exact and never decoded, and the value is decoded once. I ran independent experiments on local https mocks (127.0.0.1), reading cookies the way Next does and checking /api/admin/session, /api/admin/posts and /api/admin/posts/x in Chromium after logout. F9 passed only where Chromium ended logged out: the real-app clear, the Next Expires=1970 clear, and a Domain=localhost cookie that Chromium rejected. F9 failed on every case where Chromium stayed admin: Partitioned narrow-Path sealed, Partitioned empty-name %2A, Partitioned login with an unpartitioned clear, a Partitioned clear against an unpartitioned login, Path=/api/admin/posts/, a sealed cookie re-set by the session response after logout, and never cleared. Playwright's context.cookies() does return partitioned (CHIPS) cookies, so they are covered. A mutation that restores the old jar logic (stored name plus raw value) makes f9b-narrow-path-encoded-empty-name-smuggling-fails fail, so the test kills the regression. Launch failure fails F9 with no parser fallback, both for a bad executablePath and a bad PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_PATH. The '[SENSITIVE]' password fails fast. The bypass header is added only by an origin-filtered context.route; there is no extraHTTPHeaders or APIRequestContext. The self-test has positive controls: second-origin probes on another port and on localhost arrive without the header, and a followed-redirect control shows why redirect:'manual' is needed. In runTests only the F9 line changed. F4 goes through checkLoginCookieEntry, carried from the round-3 base, and still accepts a realistic iron-session login entry. main(), the F2 guard and the exit codes are unchanged. visual/ has no diff and docs/migration/.scratch/demo-tests is still empty. No leaks appeared in any result.
nonBlocking: docs/migration/evidence/P5.3-harness-fix.json is modified in the working tree. That file is outside this task's 'touch only' list, but the change is the round-3 parser text carried over from the starting point (the P6.1 evidence says so). The orchestrator should confirm it is intended before committing.

The jar check fails conservatively in cases where the real app would not be admin. Examples: a quoted value "<sealed>" at a narrow Path, a percent-encoded key such as growmax%2Dadmin, a key with an inner tab, a value decoded more than once. These give false fails, never false passes, and the real app's clear does not trigger any of them.

The real-origin path is unexercised: the container proxy with the SPKI pin, no ignoreHTTPSErrors, and the bypass via route.continue against Vercel (listed in notRun). Self-tests reach loopback with a proxy bypass. The first P6.2 run should confirm F9 passes against the real deployment, since F9 now makes one extra login per suite run.

F9 uses the default executable /opt/pw-browsers/chromium, a symlink to chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome. That is the same binary visual/run.mjs uses by default, so the two agree, but they spell the default path differently.

The redirect-header exposure is mitigated only by redirect:'manual' on F9's own fetches, because Playwright carries route.continue header overrides across followed redirects. Any future F9 fetch that follows redirects would leak the bypass header to the redirect target. A comment at openF9BrowserContext documents this.

blocking.issue: checkLogoutInBrowser (run.mjs:1142-1147) looks only at a cookie's stored name and raw value when it checks the jar after logout. Chromium sends a cookie with an empty name as just its value, and Next's parseCookie (node_modules/next/dist/compiled/@edge-runtime/cookies/index.js:48) runs decodeURIComponent on values. So a logout response of `growmax-admin=; Path=/; Max-Age=0; ...` plus `=growmax-admin=<sealed with %2A for *>; Path=/api/admin/posts; Secure; HttpOnly` gets past both checks. /api/admin/session never receives that cookie, so it reports isAdmin:false. The jar check sees name '' and a value that does not literally contain the sealed string. Meanwhile every request to /api/admin/posts still arrives as growmax-admin=<the sealed value> and is admin. Reproduced on a local mock: F9 pass=true and failures=[], while /api/admin/posts still sees admin=true. A fresh sealed value under an empty name at a narrow Path gets through the same way. F9 therefore does not pass only when Chromium ends logged out; this is the round-3 empty-name smuggle again, one encoding step further.
blocking.fix: Judge the jar after logout by what each cookie puts on the wire. The pair is c.name === '' ? c.value : `${c.name}=${c.value}`. Split it at the first '=' and trim SP/HTAB from the key only. If the key is growmax-admin and the value is non-empty, count the cookie as a leftover. Also compare the sealed login values against a safe decodeURIComponent of the name and value, not only the raw strings. Add self-test cases for `=growmax-admin=<%2A-encoded sealed>; Path=/api/admin/posts` and `=growmax-admin=<a different non-empty value>; Path=/api/admin/posts` next to the correct clear, and expect both to fail. Optionally also make the mock's session and posts endpoints parse cookies the way Next does: last duplicate wins, values decoded.
